summary:
A trans visitor to Vermont remains subject in full to the United States federal travel framework. Since January 2025, Executive Order 14168 has required federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth. The State Department stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth, and new passport applications are processed only as M or F according to the supporting documents submitted; passports already issued with an X marker remain valid until they expire. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some left stranded abroad. The ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, Lambda Legal maintains guidance on documentation and how name and gender changes interact with federal records, and the Supreme Court recently allowed the State Department to proceed with its changed treatment of trans passports.

Entry carries a separate exposure. Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025, titled 'Keeping Men Out of Women's Sports', was followed on 25 February 2025 by a State Department announcement that trans athletes seeking to enter the United States to compete in women's sporting events will be refused visas, with applicants flagged internally under the code 'SWS25'. The same announcement states that an applicant who declares a gender other than sex assigned at birth may be treated as fraud and barred permanently.

Checkpoint screening risks involuntary disclosure. The National Center for Transgender Equality's know-your-rights guide describes secondary screening, body scanners and pat-downs as procedures that can expose a traveller's trans status to TSA officers and other passengers, and sets out how to request a screening of the type matching one's presentation.

Within that national layer, Vermont is listed as of July 2026 among the most protective states on gender-identity nondiscrimination. The same assessment records that the federal layer is under attack through the House bathroom ban, so that tier on its own can no longer be considered most protective. Vermont also has shield laws or executive orders from the 2023 and 2024 batches that are enforceable against out-of-state action, and it appears in the nationwide directory of such jurisdictions.

Identity documents remain the fastest-moving area of restriction elsewhere in the country. Kansas has enacted a law invalidating birth certificates and driver's licences that do not bear sex assigned at birth and barring trans residents from changing those markers; rights groups describe the Kansas statute as a template other legislatures are following, with further targeting bills pending. The Movement Advancement Project's identity-document map sets out, state by state, which jurisdictions permit gender-marker changes on licences and birth certificates and under what conditions, so the rules encountered outside Vermont depend heavily on the state involved.

Facility use is regulated in a substantial number of states. State bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and some government buildings are in force in nine states and one territory, with additional states imposing outright bans on facility use according to gender identity; in some jurisdictions trans bathroom use is a criminal offence in certain circumstances. Twenty-nine states, four territories and the District of Columbia have no such ban. Enforcement is documented: in April 2025 a trans student who announced 'I am here to break the law' and used a women's restroom at the Florida state capitol was arrested and handcuffed, which civil-rights attorneys identified as the first known arrest under a state bathroom-restriction law.

Foreign governments have responded publicly to the federal document and data rules. At least eight European countries, including Finland and Denmark, adjusted travel guidelines for trans and nonbinary citizens entering the United States, and those advisories followed detentions of European citizens over visa issues.

A national legal risk assessment dated 13 July 2026 identifies Idaho as the latest state flagged do-not-travel for trans people, bringing the total to four states so designated, and records that the 2026 legislative season continued to degrade trans rights alongside the federal measures driving nationwide trends. Vermont is not among the designated states.
tangentialFactors:
Vermont's protective standing is a state-law position layered beneath a federal regime that applies regardless of destination. Non-discrimination coverage and shield protection do not alter passport issuance, visa decisions or airport screening, all of which follow national rules.

The July 2026 assessment places Vermont clearly above the national score of 0.36, and its tier is qualified by the assessment's own finding that the federal layer, including the House bathroom ban, prevents any nondiscrimination tier from being read as fully protective on its own.

Comparison across state lines is sharp. Vermont's shield laws stand against states that have moved in the opposite direction, such as Kansas on identity documents and the nine states and one territory with school and government-building bathroom bans, and against the four states flagged do-not-travel as of July 2026.

Shield protection is framed against out-of-state action, which matters for a visitor crossing a state border within the country: conduct and legal reach do not stop at the Vermont line.

outOfScopeNotes:
Vermont's specific rules and processing conditions for changing gender markers on driver's licences and birth certificates are not sourced in this inventory; only the existence of the Movement Advancement Project's state-by-state map is documented here.

Whether any enforcement action, complaint or litigation has tested Vermont's shield provisions against out-of-state action is unresolved in the sources provided.

The composition of the four states flagged do-not-travel as of the 13 July 2026 assessment is only partly resolved: Idaho is named as the latest addition, the remaining three are not identified in this inventory.

The outcome of the ACLU's challenge to the State Department's passport policy and the terms of the Supreme Court's allowance for the changed treatment are not detailed beyond the fact of the suit and the ruling.
